summary: Sell the whole bitcoin position and go back to all cash: bitcoin fell to about $68,700, its lowest since August and well under the $72,000 level I said would make me cut, so the condition for selling has been met.
thesis:
Where the account stands. The $250 bitcoin purchase decided on 12 November was made at the first price of 13 November, about $71,400. It does not appear in the account figures yet because those are only updated after the UTC day ends. At around $68,700 the holding is worth about $241, a loss of roughly $9 or 4% on the position and under 1% of the account. The other $750 is cash.

What happened today. Bitcoin's last price of 12 November was $71,370. In the first hours of 13 November it dropped through $70,000 and touched about $67,555 on Coinbase, its lowest price since mid-August, before recovering to between roughly $68,700 and $69,800 during the US day. Reports put it near $68,750 in the late afternoon UTC. The fall was sharpened by forced selling: between $1.3 billion and $1.6 billion of borrowed bets were closed out in 24 hours, almost nine tenths of them bets on rising prices. Ether fell to about $1,930, Solana to about $80 and XRP to about $1.02.

The trend. Bitcoin is now about 11% below its 20-day average ($77,220), 15% below its 50-day average ($80,860) and about 6% below its 200-day average ($73,080), the long-term line it was sitting on two days ago. It is down about 12% over 20 days. Under the plan, prices below both shorter averages and clearly below the 200-day average call for the very bottom of the 0-30% range.

The background has not improved. US spot bitcoin funds had a sixth straight day of withdrawals on 12 November (reports differ on the size, from about $48 million to $284 million), taking the run to roughly $1.5 billion. US producer prices for October rose 0.3% on the month, slightly less than feared, but the yearly rate of 6.5% is the highest since late 2022, and futures still price a Federal Reserve rate increase on 9 December as close to certain. The dollar is near a 19-month high and the 10-year US government bond yield is around 5.15%, both of which tend to weigh on crypto. Trading is thin, so moves in either direction are exaggerated.

Why sell rather than wait. Yesterday I wrote that I would sell at least half if 13 November ended below about $72,000, and all of it if the price was heading toward the August low near $69,300. The price went through both levels. The runbook says that when a stated condition for selling is met, I sell, and asked fresh whether I would buy bitcoin today under this plan, the answer is no: the plan buys strength and this is weakness. I am selling all of it rather than half because the position is small either way, and a half-measure would mostly be a way of avoiding the decision.

The honest case against selling. This is exactly the sort of moment when prices often bounce. The Fear and Greed index is at 20, its lowest since July; the cost of holding borrowed bets has turned negative, meaning traders are leaning toward further falls; a large flush of forced selling has just happened; and the price is sitting on its 200-week average near $67,750, a level where long-term buyers have stepped in before. A sharp rebound from here is quite possible and I would miss it. I accept that because the plan's working assumption is that trends persist, and I would rather test that assumption cleanly than abandon it on the first hard day. The cost of being wrong is small: buying back in costs about 0.3% plus whatever the price has risen.

No other coin earns a place. Every coin on the watch list is below its 20-day and 50-day averages, most have fallen further than bitcoin over the past month, and none has news of its own.

What would bring me back. I will buy bitcoin again if it ends a UTC day back above its 200-day average, near $73,100, or earlier with a smaller amount if it holds above $70,000 for two UTC days while the bitcoin funds start taking in money again. If instead it falls further, the next levels others are watching are about $64,100 (the 19 August low) and about $60,000; I would not buy just because the price is lower, only once it stops falling and turns.
risks: The main risk is selling near a short-term low: fear is extreme and forced selling has just cleared out many borrowed bets, so a rebound could start at any time, and with no bitcoin at all the account would fall behind the benchmark quickly. The sale is made at the first price of 14 November, which could be noticeably above or below today's levels; weekend trading is thin and can move sharply. A Federal Reserve speech on 14 November, inflation data on 25 November and the rate decision on 9 December could each move prices either way. Today's prices come from news reports published up to the late afternoon UTC, not from the exchange itself, and reports disagree on the size of the fund withdrawals.

orders.reason: Bitcoin broke below $72,000 and the August low near $69,300, the conditions set yesterday for selling; the trend is down on every measure in the plan.
